claim: Seven hundred and eight participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were studied.
source: Seven hundred and eight participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were studied.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants and their source in the abstract.

claim: Individual-level structural and metabolic covariance scores in higher-level cognitive and hippocampal networks were derived from magnetic resonance imaging and [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography using seed-based partial least square analyses.
source: Individual-level structural and metabolic covariance scores in higher-level cognitive and hippocampal networks were derived from magnetic resonance imaging and [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography using seed-based partial least square analyses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology used to derive network scores from imaging data.

claim: The non-linear associations between network scores and memory across cognitive stages in each pathology group were examined using sparse varying coefficient modelling.
source: The non-linear associations between network scores and memory across cognitive stages in each pathology group were examined using sparse varying coefficient modelling.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the analytical method used to examine associations.

claim: In amyloid pathology group, there was an early influence of hippocampal structural network deterioration on memory impairment in the preclinical stage.
source: In amyloid pathology group, there was an early influence of hippocampal structural network deterioration on memory impairment in the preclinical stage
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from the SVC modeling showing early hippocampal network influence in preclinical AD.

claim: There was a biphasic influence of the angular gyrus-seeded default mode metabolic network on memory in both preclinical and dementia stages in the amyloid pathology group.
source: a biphasic influence of the angular gyrus-seeded default mode metabolic network on memory in both preclinical and dementia stages
evidence: The manuscript reports a biphasic pattern of association between ANG metabolic network and memory across disease stages.

claim: In non-amyloid pathology groups, the trajectory of the hippocampus-memory association was opposite and weaker overall compared to amyloid pathology groups.
source: In non-amyloid pathology groups, in contrast, the trajectory of the hippocampus-memory association was opposite and weaker overall
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the hippocampus-memory association trajectories between amyloid and non-amyloid groups.

claim: No metabolism covariance networks were related to memory in non-amyloid pathology groups.
source: while no metabolism covariance networks were related to memory
evidence: The manuscript states that metabolic networks did not show associations with memory in non-amyloid groups.

claim: Key findings were replicated in a larger cohort of 1280 participants.
source: Key findings were replicated in a larger cohort of 1280 participants.
evidence: The manuscript reports replication of findings in a validation dataset.

claim: Data collection and sharing for this project was funded by the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (National Institutes of Health Grant U01 AG024904) and DOD ADNI (Department of Defense award number W81XWH-12-2-0012).
source: Data collection and sharing for this project was funded by the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (National Institutes of Health Grant U01 AG024904) and DOD ADNI (Department of Defense award number W81XWH-12-2-0012).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists funding sources in the abstract.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by neuropathological accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, intraneuronal tau neurofibrillary tangles, and neurodegeneration in the brain.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease that is characterised by neuropathological accumulation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques (A), intraneuronal tau neurofibrillary tangles (T), and neurodegeneration (N) in the brain (Braak and Braak, 1991; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on AD pathology.

claim: The AT(N) system has been proposed as a biological construct for Alzheimer's disease based on biomarkers.
source: the emerging development of biomarkers to profile AD pathophysiology has led to the proposal of AD as a biological construct based on the AT(N) system (Jack et al., 2016; Jack et al., 2018)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing the AT(N) classification system.

claim: Aβ is the first to become abnormal in AD, followed by downstream pathophysiological changes of tauopathy, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment.
source: Studies have suggested that Aβ is the ﬁrst to become abnormal in AD, followed by downstream pathophysiological changes of tauopathy, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment (Bateman et al., 2012; Jack et al., 2013a; Bertens et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting the temporal sequence of AD pathology.

claim: Neurodegeneration represents neuronal injury in the forms of cerebral grey matter atrophy and hypometabolism.
source: Neurodegeneration represents neuronal injury in the forms of cerebral grey matter (GM) atrophy and hypometabolism.
evidence: The manuscript defines neurodegeneration based on established knowledge.

claim: In AD, Aβ triggers tau-mediated toxicity leading to AD-type neurodegeneration in brain regions such as the hippocampus, the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex, bilateral angular gyrus, and medial temporal lobes.
source: In AD, it is widely postulated that Aβ triggers tau-mediated toxicity leading to AD-type neurodegeneration in brain regions such as the hippocampus, the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), bilateral angular gyrus (ANG), and medial temporal lobes (Chételat et al., 2008; Misra et al., 2009; Mosconi et al., 2009; Kljajevic et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the cascade of AD pathology in specific brain regions.

claim: Amyloid and tau pathologies have a synergistic effect on AD-type hypometabolism, involving the basal and mesial temporal, orbitofrontal, and anterior and posterior cingulate cortices.
source: Recently, amyloid and tau pathologies are also shown to have a synergistic effect on AD-type hypometabolism, involving the basal and mesial temporal, orbitofrontal, and anterior and posterior cingulate cortices (Hanseeuw et al., 2017; Pascoal et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies on the synergistic effects of amyloid and tau.

claim: Neurodegeneration may occur prior to incident amyloid positivity.
source: However, neurodegeneration may also occur prior to incident amyloid positivity (Jack et al., 2013b)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing neurodegeneration can precede amyloid accumulation.

claim: Neurodegeneration may be influenced by the loss of microtubule stabilising function and toxic effects of tau pathology, independent of amyloid pathology.
source: be influenced by the loss of microtubule stabilising function and toxic effects of tau pathology, independent of amyloid pathology (Ballatore et al., 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on tau-mediated neurodegeneration independent of amyloid.

claim: AD pathophysiology compromises brain structure and function systematically by capitalizing on the intrinsic connectivities among brain regions.
source: Work from our group has demonstrated that AD pathophysiologies compromise brain structure and function systematically by capitalising on the intrinsic connectivities among brain regions (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work from the research group on network effects of AD.

claim: AD pathological deposition around neurons impairs synaptic communication and leads to specific large-scale brain intrinsic network disorganisation.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that AD pathological deposition around neurons which impairs synaptic communication, leads to specific large-scale brain intrinsic network disorganisation (Seeley et al., 2009; Marchitelli et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on how AD pathology affects brain networks.

claim: Decreased functional connectivity in the default mode network is well-described in MCI and AD.
source: Decreased functional connectivity in the default mode network (DMN) derived from resting state functional MRI is well-described in MCI and AD (Greicius et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2010; Chong et al., 2017; Chong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies documenting DMN dysfunction in AD.

claim: Aberrant loss of functional connectivity in executive control network and salience network are being increasingly reported in AD.
source: while aberrant loss of functional connectivity in other higher-order cognitive networks such as the executive control network (ECN) and salience network (SN) are being increasingly reported (Chong et al., 2017; Brier et al., 2012; He et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on ECN and SN dysfunction in AD.

claim: Brain networks can be constructed based on similarity in GM structure and metabolism between brain areas across individuals, known as the GM structural and metabolic covariance network.
source: Brain networks can also be constructed based on similarity in GM structure and metabolism between brain areas across individuals, known as the GM structural and metabolic covariance network, respectively (Ripp et al., 2020; Zielinski et al., 2010; Montembeault et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature defining structural and metabolic covariance networks.

claim: Structural and metabolic covariance networks show convergent patterns with the intrinsic connectivity network in healthy individuals.
source: Both structural and metabolic covariance networks show convergent patterns with the intrinsic connectivity network in healthy individuals and mirror GM atrophy patterns in distinct neurodegenerative disorders (Seeley et al., 2009; Ripp et al., 2020; Lizarraga et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing convergence between different network modalities.

claim: A recent study revealed differential patterns of structural covariance networks within different amyloid pathology groups classified by cerebrospinal fluid Aβ1–42 and P-tau181 levels.
source: Using this approach, a recent study revealed differential patterns of structural covariance networks within different amyloid pathology groups classified by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Aβ1–42 and P-tau181 levels (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on structural covariance networks in different pathology groups.

claim: Network analysis at the individual level allows direct evaluation of each individual's structural and metabolic covariance networks.
source: It is postulated that network analysis at the individual level will allow direct evaluation of each individual's structural and metabolic covariance networks, hence providing deeper understanding on the effects of brain networks on cognitive performances (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the advantages of individual-level network analysis.

claim: Single-subject GM graph properties were associated with individual differences of clinical progression in AD.
source: a cube-based correlation approach to calculate the individual GM networks by computing intracortical similarities in GM morphology (Tijms et al., 2012) showed that single-subject GM graph properties were associated with individual differences of clinical progression in AD (Tijms et al., 2018; Tijms et al., 2014; Vermunt et al., 2020; Tijms et al., 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing associations between individual network properties and AD progression.

claim: The influence of cerebral GM loss and [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose hypometabolism on cognitive function in AD has often been modelled as a linear relationship.
source: The influence of cerebral GM loss and [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) hypometabolism on cognitive function in AD has often been modelled as a linear relationship (Habeck et al., 2012; Bejanin et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on linear modeling approaches in AD research.

claim: Structural and metabolic abnormalities in AD may follow a sigmoidal curve trajectory with an initial period of acceleration and subsequent deceleration.
source: However, emerging evidence suggests that structural and metabolic abnormalities in AD may follow a sigmoidal curve trajectory with an initial period of acceleration and subsequent deceleration (Jack et al., 2013a; Sabuncu et al., 2011; Schuff et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature suggesting non-linear trajectories of AD biomarkers.

claim: The dynamic effects of AD biomarkers on worsening cognition can be better modelled by sigmoid-shaped curves rather than a constant across disease stages.
source: While the dynamic effects of AD biomarkers on worsening cognition can be better modelled by sigmoid-shaped curves rather than a constant across disease stages (Caroli et al., 2010)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting non-linear modeling of biomarker-cognition relationships.

claim: The seed partial least squares method was used to evaluate individual-level brain network integrity.
source: We used the seed partial least squares (PLS) method (Krishnan et al., 2011) to evaluate the individual-level brain network integrity.
evidence: The manuscript cites the methodological approach used for network analysis.

claim: The sparse varying coefficient model does not assume a constant relationship between brain measures and cognitive performance over different cognitive stages.
source: We employed the sparse varying coefficient (SVC) model which does not assume a constant relationship between brain measures and cognitive performance over different cognitive stages (Hong et al., 2015; Daye et al., 2012; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the SVC modeling approach and its key feature.

claim: Individual-level brain metabolic and structural network integrity would be non-linearly associated with memory performance across the AD continuum.
source: We hypothesised that individual-level brain metabolic and structural network integrity would be non-linearly associated with memory performance across the AD continuum and such trajectories would vary depending on the presence of amyloid and tau protein deposition.
evidence: The manuscript states the primary hypothesis of the study.

claim: The posterior DMN and the medial temporal lobe regions would play an early and dominant role affecting memory performance in individuals with amyloid pathology.
source: Based on our previous findings (Zhou et al., 2010; Chong et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020), we further hypothesised that the posterior DMN and the medial temporal lobe regions would play an early and dominant role affecting the memory performance in individuals with amyloid pathology.
evidence: The manuscript states a hypothesis based on prior work from the research group.

claim: Both hippocampal structural and ANG metabolic network integrity contributed to memory performance in the early cognitively normal stage in individuals with amyloid deposition.
source: Our study provides first evidence that both hippocampal structural and ANG metabolic network integrity contributed to memory performance in the early cognitively normal stage in individuals with amyloid deposition.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings from the study.

claim: In amyloid positive individuals with dementia, only the ANG metabolic network dominated the memory-network association.
source: However, in the amyloid positive individuals with dementia, only the ANG metabolic network dominated the memory-network association.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings specific to the dementia stage in amyloid positive individuals.

claim: Amyloid negative individuals did not have the patterns of network-memory associations observed in amyloid positive individuals.
source: Amyloid negative individuals did not have such patterns.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts findings between amyloid positive and negative groups.

claim: 812 participants (232 CN, 413 MCI, and 167 probable AD) were selected from the ADNI database with 3T T1-weighted MRI and [18F]FDG PET scans to define seed regions for brain network derivation.
source: We selected 812 participants (232 CN, 413 MCI, and 167 probable AD) from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database with 3T T1-weighted MRI and [18F]FDG PET scans to define seed regions for brain network derivation (Figure 1, step 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the participant selection and references a figure showing the workflow.

claim: The DMN included bilateral ANG, PCC, and medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Specifically, the DMN included bilateral ANG, PCC, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)
evidence: The manuscript defines the regions comprising the DMN.

claim: The SN included bilateral anterior insular.
source: the SN included bilateral anterior insular (INS)
evidence: The manuscript defines the regions comprising the SN.

claim: The ECN included bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortex.
source: the ECN included bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC)
evidence: The manuscript defines the regions comprising the ECN.

claim: The memory network included bilateral HIP.
source: the memory network included bilateral HIP
evidence: The manuscript defines the regions comprising the memory network.

claim: The seed coordinates were determined based on the group comparisons of the grey matter volume probability and glucose metabolic spatial maps between CN and probable AD individuals.
source: The seed coordinates were determined based on the group comparisons of the grey matter volume (GMV) probability and glucose metabolic spatial maps between CN and probable AD individuals (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 4, see details in Methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for determining seed coordinates.

claim: The main study cohort was stratified into three pathology groups: A-T- (non-amyloid/non-tau), A-T+ (tau only) and A+T-/A+T+ (amyloid pathology).
source: Using the ADNI published cutoffs of Aβ1-42<192 pg/mL and CSF p-tau181p >23 pg/mL to define the presence of Aβ and tau pathology, respectively (Shaw et al., 2009), the main study cohort was further stratified into three pathology groups: A-T- (non-amyloid/non-tau), A-T+ (tau only) and A+T-/A+T + (amyloid pathology; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pathology-based stratification using established cutoffs.

claim: In participants with amyloid pathology (A+T-/A+T+), the probable AD group had lower metabolic and structural network scores than the CN and MCI groups in all the networks.
source: In participants with amyloid pathology (A+T-/A+T + ), the probable AD group had lower metabolic and structural network scores than the CN and MCI groups in all the networks (Figure 2B right and 3B right).
evidence: The manuscript reports group differences in network scores and references figures showing the data.

claim: No difference in metabolic and structural network scores was observed in participants without amyloid pathology across cognitive stages.
source: No such difference was observed in participants without amyloid pathology.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of group differences in non-amyloid groups.

claim: Amyloid positive MCI individuals had lower metabolic and structural network scores than the MCI individuals without amyloid and tau pathology for all the networks.
source: Specifically, at the same cognitive stage, amyloid positive (A+T-/A+T + ) MCI individuals had lower metabolic and structural network scores than the MCI individuals without amyloid and tau pathology (A-T-) for all the networks (Figures 2B and 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports differences in network scores between pathology groups at the same cognitive stage.

claim: Amyloid positive CN individuals had comparable structural network scores but lower metabolic network scores than the CN individuals without amyloid and tau pathology.
source: The amyloid positive CN individuals had comparable structural network scores but lower metabolic network scores than the CN individuals without amyloid and tau pathology.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential patterns in structural vs metabolic networks in CN individuals.

claim: CN individuals with amyloid pathology showed lower structural integrity in the HIP-based memory network, the mPFC-based anterior DMN and the INS-based SN than the CN individuals with tau pathology only.
source: In contrast, CN individuals with amyloid pathology (A+T-/A+T + ) showed lower structural integrity in the HIP-based memory network, the mPFC-based anterior DMN and the INS-based SN than the CN individuals with tau pathology only (A-T+).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific network differences between amyloid and tau-only CN groups.

claim: CN individuals with tau pathology had lower structural mPFC-based anterior DMN scores than the CN group without tau and amyloid pathology.
source: In addition, CN individuals with tau pathology (A-T+) had lower structural mPFC-based anterior DMN scores than the CN group without tau and amyloid pathology (A-T-).
evidence: The manuscript reports differences in mPFC network scores between tau-positive and negative CN groups.

claim: The HIP-based structural memory network score was identified as a key predictor of memory impairment in all three pathology groups.
source: The SVC models identified the HIP-based structural memory network score as a key predictor of memory impairment in all three pathology groups (Figures 4A and 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from SVC modeling and references figures showing the results.

claim: Lower HIP structural network scores were associated with lower ADNI-mem scores.
source: We found that the lower HIP structural network scores, the lower the ADNI-mem scores (indicated by positive beta coefficient).
evidence: The manuscript reports the direction of association between HIP network and memory.

claim: The strength of the HIP-memory association was higher in the amyloid pathology group than the other two A-groups.
source: The strength of this association was higher (i.e. higher beta coefficient) in the amyloid pathology group than the other two A-groups.
evidence: The manuscript compares the strength of associations across pathology groups.

claim: In the amyloid pathology group, the strength of the HIP-memory association was highest in early CN stage, and decreased from late CN to early MCI stage.
source: Specifically, in the amyloid pathology group, the strength of this association was highest in early CN stage, and decreased from late CN to early MCI stage (Figure 4A, left).
evidence: The manuscript describes the trajectory of the HIP-memory association in amyloid positive individuals.

claim: In the A-T- group, the strength of the HIP-memory association was lowest in early CN stage and increased in the late CN stage.
source: Specifically, in the A-T- group, the strength of the association between the HIP structural network and memory performance was lowest in early CN stage and increased in the late CN stage.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trajectory of the HIP-memory association in the A-T- group.

claim: In the A-T+ group, the strength of the HIP-memory association was low in the CN stage and gradually increased in the MCI stage, reaching the highest in the late MCI and dementia stage.
source: Similarly, in the A-T +group, the strength of such association was low in the CN stage and gradually increased in the MCI stage, reaching the highest in the late MCI and dementia stage.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trajectory of the HIP-memory association in the A-T+ group.

claim: The ANG-based metabolic network score was associated with memory impairment only in the amyloid pathology group.
source: The SVC models identified the ANG-based metabolic network score (i.e. DMN) to be associated with memory impairment only in the amyloid pathology group (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from SVC modeling specific to the amyloid group.

claim: Lower ANG metabolic network scores were associated with lower ADNI-mem scores.
source: We found that the lower the ANG metabolic network score, the lower the ADNI-mem score.
evidence: The manuscript reports the direction of association between ANG network and memory.

claim: The strength of the ANG-memory relationship showed an early peak in early CN and gradually decreased in the late CN and MCI stages, before increasing in late MCI/dementia stage again.
source: The strength of this relationship showed an early peak in early CN and gradually decreased in the late CN and MCI stages, before increasing in late MCI/dementia stage again.
evidence: The manuscript describes the biphasic trajectory of the ANG-memory association.

claim: A larger validation dataset was created by including another 468 individuals who underwent 1.5T T1-weighted MRI scan.
source: To test if the above findings from the main dataset can be replicated, we repeated the same analyses using a larger validation dataset (here after refer as validation dataset 1). We added an additional 468 individuals who underwent 1.5T T1-weighted MRI scans and [18F]FDG PET.
evidence: The manuscript describes the validation dataset composition.

claim: The validation dataset 1 included 1280 participants in total for brain seed definition.
source: With the original main dataset of 812 participants, we had 1280 participants in total for brain seed definition (Figure 1, step 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the total sample size for validation analyses.

claim: Most key findings were replicated in validation dataset 1.
source: We performed the same PLS-SVC analyses on validation dataset 1 and replicated most of our key findings (Figures 4B and 5B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports successful replication of findings and references multiple figures.

claim: The HIP-based structural memory network and the ANG-based metabolic DMN scores were associated with memory impairment in the respective pathology groups with similar beta curves as the main dataset in validation dataset 1.
source: Specifically, the HIP-based structural memory network and the ANG-based metabolic DMN scores were associated with memory impairment in the respective pathology groups with similar beta curves as the main dataset.
evidence: The manuscript reports consistency of findings between main and validation datasets.

claim: Findings remained robust when analyses were performed using the alternative ordering strategy of merging both MCI and dementia stages.
source: Furthermore, these observations remained robust when the analyses were performed using the alternative ordering strategy of merging both MCI and dementia stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C & Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports robustness of findings to different ordering methods.

claim: Validation dataset 2 analysis on the A+T-/A+T+ group revealed consistent findings as the main dataset.
source: Moreover, we also repeated the same analyses using only the 468 independent individuals (here after refer as validation dataset 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Due to the small sample sizes of the A-T- and A-T +groups, we only performed the SVC modelling on the A+T-/A+T + group, which revealed consistent findings (i.e. predictors and stage-dependent trajectories) as the main dataset (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation in an independent dataset.

claim: Results were consistent when PLS was performed on the CN group only to generate the group-level brain salience maps.
source: To test whether the results were sensitised to the relative imbalance of group sizes across diagnoses, we repeated the same analyses in the validation dataset 1 by performing PLS on the CN group only to generate the group-level brain salience maps in a healthy cohort. The individual brain glucose metabolic and grey matter probably spatial maps were then projected onto these CN-derived salience maps to generate the individual brain network scores. The subsequent SVC modelling replicated most of our key findings from the main dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports robustness of findings to different reference group selection.

claim: Permutation tests showed high specificity of the established SVC models.
source: Last, we evaluated the specificity of the established SVC models using permutation tests. For each null SVC model using the permuted datasets, the frequency distributions of variable selection (i.e. the total times of selection as the key predictor of memory scores within the 100 permuted datasets) appeared random (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). As the selected variables in our main findings were not favoured over the other variables in the null models, this indicated the high specificity of the SVC models that were built on the original dataset.
evidence: The manuscript reports results of permutation testing for model specificity.

claim: Results obtained with LASSO or Ridge as the penalty in the SVC modelling were consistent.
source: To further evaluate the specificity and robustness of the SVC models, we replaced LASSO with Ridge as the penalty in the SVC modelling. All results obtained on the main dataset with either LASSO or Ridge as the penalty in the SVC modelling were consistent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D & Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports robustness of findings to different penalty methods.

claim: The hippocampus plays a role in memory cognitive domain.
source: The HIP structural network is identified to be associated with memory impairment in all three pathology groups which is consistent with the role that the hippocampus plays in memory cognitive domain (Tulving and Markowitsch, 1998; Eichenbaum, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the hippocampus role in memory.

claim: A recent study showed that the AD model for hippocampus diverged early from normal aging trajectory.
source: Our findings are in line with a recent study that compared MRI brain structure models of normal and AD participants across the entire lifespan, showing that the AD model for hippocampus diverged early from normal aging trajectory (Coupé et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting early hippocampal changes in AD.

claim: Hippocampal volume and thickness are early imaging correlates of verbal memory in preclinical AD.
source: Accumulating evidence also suggests hippocampal volume and thickness as early imaging correlates of verbal memory in preclinical AD (Bayram et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites evidence for early hippocampal changes in preclinical AD.

claim: In a cohort of CN individuals, decreased CSF Aβ42 was associated with hippocampal loss and poorer performance on episodic memory.
source: Furthermore, in a cohort of CN individuals, decreased CSF Aβ42 was associated with hippocampal loss and poorer performance on episodic memory (Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study linking amyloid, hippocampal atrophy, and memory in CN individuals.

claim: An early effect of Aβ on memory mediated by hippocampal atrophy has been demonstrated in non-demented older individuals.
source: while an early effect of Aβ on memory mediated by hippocampal atrophy has been demonstrated in non-demented older individuals (Mormino et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2015; Mattsson et al., 2015)
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing amyloid effects on memory via hippocampal atrophy.

claim: The hippocampus system is well connected to various cortical brain regions in processing memory information.
source: Indeed, the hippocampus system is well connected to various cortical brain regions in processing memory information (Treves and Rolls, 1994)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on hippocampal connectivity.

claim: The hippocampus together with brain structures such as the prefrontal cortex make up a large-scale network to support encoding and retrieval of episodic memory.
source: and together with brain structures such as the prefrontal cortex make up a large-scale network to support encoding and retrieval of episodic memory (Blumenfeld and Ranganath, 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the memory network.

claim: Grey matter regions outside the medial temporal lobes are gradually implicated as AD progresses to MCI and dementia.
source: While the medial temporal lobe is well known to be affected early on in the AD process, grey matter regions outside the medial temporal lobes are gradually implicated as the disease progresses to MCI and dementia (Bayram et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the progression of brain atrophy in AD.

claim: Atrophy in brain regions within the DMN such as the precuneus and the posterior cingulate gyrus are associated with episodic memory impairment.
source: Atrophy in brain regions within the DMN such as the precuneus and the posterior cingulate gyrus are shown to be associated with episodic memory impairment (Doré et al., 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study linking DMN atrophy to memory impairment.

claim: Decreased inferior frontal gyrus volume is associated with verbal memory decline in MCI patients who converted to AD over time.
source: and decreased inferior frontal gyrus volume is associated with verbal memory decline in MCI patients who converted to AD over time (Defrancesco et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on frontal atrophy and memory decline in MCI converters.

claim: Impaired glucose uptake in the ANG is consistently shown to be an important feature for predicting memory and executive functioning performance in the later stages of AD.
source: While impaired glucose uptake in the ANG is consistently shown to be an important feature for predicting memory and executive functioning performance in the later stages of AD (Jeong et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2020)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on ANG hypometabolism in later AD stages.

claim: The ANG is one of the major connector hubs that links different subsystems such as the DMN.
source: The ANG, located in the posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, is one of the major connector hubs that links different subsystems such as the DMN (Greicius et al., 2004; Tomasi and Volkow, 2011) that are affected by AD pathophysiology
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the ANG as a network hub.

claim: The ANG is involved in verbal working memory and episodic memory retrieval.
source: and is involved in verbal working memory (Jonides et al., 1998; Seghier, 2013) and episodic memory retrieval (Ciaramelli et al., 2008)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on ANG functions in memory.

claim: The ANG has strong connectivity with the hippocampal system.
source: The role of ANG in memory performance is also implicated by its strong connectivity with the hippocampal system (Seghier, 2013) that is critical in episodic and declarative memory functions Tulving and Markowitsch, 1998.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on ANG-hippocampus connectivity.

claim: Aβ aggregation within the brain's DMN is associated with regional hypometabolism in distant but functionally connected brain regions, including the inferior parietal cortices.
source: Furthermore, a recent study showed that Aβ aggregation within the brain's DMN is associated with regional hypometabolism in distant but functionally connected brain regions, including the inferior parietal cortices where the ANG is located (Pascoal et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study linking amyloid to hypometabolism in connected regions.

claim: Among amnestic MCI individuals, increased FC compared to controls was found within the DMN and between DMN and brain networks such as the frontoparietal control and dorsal attention networks.
source: Among amnestic MCI individuals, increased FC compared to controls was found within the DMN and between DMN and brain networks such as the frontoparietal control and dorsal attention networks.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on increased connectivity in MCI.

claim: Abnormal increased FC patterns in MCI are associated with lower cognitive performance which suggest a maladaptive compensatory mechanism.
source: These abnormal increased FC patterns are associated with lower cognitive performance which suggest a maladaptive compensatory mechanism in the MCI stage (Gardini et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies suggesting maladaptive compensation in MCI.

claim: Higher nodal topological properties and increased local and medium-range connectivity located in the DMN-related brain regions were shown in the earlier subjective cognitive decline stage of AD relative to healthy controls.
source: Similarly, higher nodal topological properties such as the nodal strength, nodal global efficiency and nodal local efficiency, and increased local and medium-range connectivity located in the DMN-related brain regions were also shown in the earlier subjective cognitive decline stage of AD relative to healthy controls (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on network changes in subjective cognitive decline.

claim: A recent study on 531 deceased older community adults showed that neuropathologies such as AD, cerebrovascular disease and hippocampal sclerosis accounted for 42.6% of the variation in global cognitive decline.
source: In line with our finding, a recent study on 531 deceased older community adults showed that neuropathologies such as AD, cerebrovascular disease and hippocampal sclerosis accounted for 42.6% of the variation in global cognitive decline, whereas hippocampal volume alone only accounted for an additional 5.4% of this variation (Dawe et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the contribution of various pathologies to cognitive decline.

claim: Hippocampal atrophy is associated with memory deficits even before the presence of dementia and can predict dementia progression.
source: Although prior studies have consistently demonstrated that hippocampal atrophy is associated with memory deficits even before the presence of dementia and can predict dementia progression (Ferrarini et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on hippocampal atrophy and memory/dementia.

claim: The relationship between hippocampal atrophy and memory is dependent on factors such as age and cognitive reserve.
source: emerging evidence suggests that the relationship between hippocampal atrophy and memory is also dependent on other factors such as age and cognitive reserve (Gorbach et al., 2017; Vuoksimaa et al., 2013; Svenningsson et al., 2019)
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing moderation of hippocampus-memory relationship by other factors.

claim: The association between episodic-memory decline and atrophy in the hippocampus over time was stronger in older than in the middle-aged participants.
source: Specifically, the association between episodic-memory decline and atrophy in the hippocampus over time was stronger in older than in the middle-aged participants (Gorbach et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing age-dependent hippocampus-memory associations.

claim: In middle age, hippocampal volume was related to memory in those with low cognitive reserve, but not in those with high cognitive reserve.
source: In middle age, hippocampal volume was related to memory in those with low cognitive reserve, but not in those with high cognitive reserve (Vuoksimaa et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing cognitive reserve moderation of hippocampus-memory relationship.

claim: The ADNI cohort consists of self-selected individuals participating in a study focusing on AD research, which may introduce selection bias.
source: First, the ADNI cohort consists of self-selected individuals participating in a study focusing on AD research, e.g., relatively more amyloid positive individuals, which may introduce selection bias and limit the generalisability of our findings to a broader community.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation regarding potential selection bias.

claim: The study design is cross-sectional thus provides only indirect evidence on the underlying brain-behaviour relationship.
source: Second, our study design is cross-sectional thus provides only indirect evidence on the underlying brain-behaviour relationship.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the cross-sectional nature as a limitation.

claim: All participants from the main dataset underwent T1-weighted MRI scans according to the standardised ADNI protocol using 3-Tesla scanners.
source: All participants from the main dataset underwent T1-weighted MRI scans according to the standardised ADNI protocol using 3-Tesla scanners.
evidence: The manuscript describes the imaging protocol for the main dataset.

claim: All participants underwent [18F]FDG PET to study cerebral glucose metabolism (185 MBq (5 mCi), dynamic 3D scan of six 5 min frames 30–60 min postinjection).
source: All participants also underwent [18F]FDG PET to study cerebral glucose metabolism (185 MBq (5 mCi), dynamic 3D scan of six 5 min frames 30–60 min postinjection).
evidence: The manuscript describes the FDG-PET imaging protocol.

claim: All T1-weighted MRI scans were corrected for field distortions and processed using the CIVET image processing pipeline.
source: All T1-weighted MRI scans were corrected for field distortions and processed using the CIVET image processing pipeline (https://www.bic.mni.mcgill.ca/ServicesSoftware/CIVET) to generate the GM probability maps as previously described (Kang et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MRI preprocessing pipeline.

claim: [18F]FDG PET images were processed with an in-house processing pipeline.
source: [18F]FDG PET images were processed with an in-house processing pipeline as described in our previous work (Nilson et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the PET preprocessing pipeline and cites prior work.

claim: CN was defined as those with MMSE scores ≥24 and CDR 0, and showed no signs of depression, MCI, or dementia.
source: Following ADNI diagnostic criteria (Petersen et al., 2010), we defined CN as those with mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores ≥24 and clinical dementia rating (CDR) 0, and showed no signs of depression, MCI, or dementia.
evidence: The manuscript defines the CN group criteria based on ADNI standards.

claim: MCI was defined as those with MMSE scores ≥24 and CDR 0.5, subjective and objective memory loss, absence of significant levels of impairment in other cognitive domains, essentially preserved activities of daily living, and an absence of dementia.
source: MCI was defined as those with MMSE scores ≥24 and CDR 0.5, subjective and objective memory loss, absence of significant levels of impairment in other cognitive domains, essentially preserved activities of daily living, and an absence of dementia.
evidence: The manuscript defines the MCI group criteria based on ADNI standards.

claim: Probable AD was defined as those with MMSE scores ≤26, CDR ≥0.5 and meeting the NINCDS/ADRDA criteria for probable AD.
source: Probable AD was defined as those with MMSE scores ≤26, CDR ≥0.5 and meeting the NINCDS/ADRDA criteria for probable AD.
evidence: The manuscript defines the probable AD group criteria.

claim: The ADNI published cutoffs of Aβ1-42<192 pg/mL and CSF p-tau181p >23 pg/mL were used to define the presence of Aβ and tau pathology.
source: Using the ADNI published cutoffs of Aβ1-42<192 pg/mL and CSF p-tau181p >23 pg/mL to define the presence of Aβ and tau pathology, respectively (Shaw et al., 2009)
evidence: The manuscript cites the established cutoffs for pathology classification.

claim: The ADNI-mem is a validated composite memory score derived using data from the ADNI neuropsychological battery.
source: The ADNI-mem is a validated composite memory score derived using data from the ADNI neuropsychological battery (Crane et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites the source of the memory composite score.

claim: The ADNI study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of all of the participating institutions and informed written consent was obtained from all participants at each site.
source: The ADNI study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of all of the participating institutions and informed written consent was obtained from all participants at each site.
evidence: The manuscript states ethical approval and consent procedures.

claim: Seed PLS was used to identify covariance patterns between GMV/metabolism in each seed region and those of all other voxels in the whole brain.
source: We used seed PLS to identify covariance patterns between GMV/metabolism in each seed region and those of all other voxels in the whole brain (Figure 1, step 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the PLS methodology.

claim: The resulting significant LV from the PLS analyses of each of the 12 seeds corresponded to reliable patterns of structural or metabolic covariance network associated with that seed.
source: The resulting significant LV from the PLS analyses of each of the 12 seeds (all p<0.0001) corresponded to reliable patterns of structural or metabolic covariance network associated with that seed (see Figure 2A, Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of PLS results and references figures.

claim: Each participant had 14 brain network scores (two for each of the 7 seed regions), which reflect structural or metabolic network pattern expression.
source: In total, each participant had 14 brain network scores (i.e. two for each of the 7 seed regions, including HIP, ANG, PCC, mPFC, INS, PPC, and DLPFC), which reflect structural or metabolic network pattern expression.
evidence: The manuscript describes the number and nature of network scores derived for each participant.

claim: Brain measures that were consistently selected by more than 90 repetitions in SVC modeling were interpreted as critical brain networks contributing to memory.
source: We ran each SVC model for 100 repetitions and reported the brain measures that were consistently selected by more than 90 repetitions. These measures were interpreted as a set of critical brain GMV/metabolism networks that contributed to memory across the cognitive stages, with a vector of beta coefficients reflecting stage-dependent (non)linearity in the network-memory association.
evidence: The manuscript describes the criterion for identifying key predictors in SVC models.

claim: Participants were ordered by their cognitive stages (CN → MCI → dementia) in each of the three pathology groups for SVC modeling.
source: To characterise the possible stage-dependent trajectories using SVC modelling, we ordered the participants by their cognitive stages (i.e. CN → MCI → dementia; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) in each of the three pathology groups (A-/T-, A-/T+and A+T-/A+T + ).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ordering method for SVC analysis.

claim: Within each cognitive stage, participants were ordered by their global cognition or dementia severity.
source: Within each stage, the participants were then ordered by their global cognition or dementia severity (i.e. no impairment → severe impairment). Specifically, the participants within the CN group were ordered by decreasing MMSE scores, while the participants within the MCI and dementia groups were ordered by increasing CDR-sum of boxes (SOB) scores.
evidence: The manuscript describes the within-stage ordering method.

claim: Participants with the same MMSE or CDR-SOB scores were further ordered by increasing age.
source: Participants with the same MMSE or CDR-SOB scores were further ordered by increasing age (i.e. young → old).
evidence: The manuscript describes the tertiary ordering criterion.

claim: Ordered participants were distributed evenly into bins (10 subjects/bin) for SVC modeling.
source: Ordered participants were distributed evenly into bins (i.e. 10 subjects/bin).
evidence: The manuscript describes the binning procedure for SVC analysis.

claim: In SVC models, the dependent variable was the ADNI memory composite score.
source: In our SVC models, the dependent variable was the ADNI memory composite score.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the outcome variable in SVC models.

claim: Predictors in SVC models included all the 14 FDG/GMV regional network scores with gender, education years, APOE ε4, intracranial volume, and scanning site as nuisance variables.
source: Predictors included all the 14 FDG/GMV regional network scores with gender, education years, APOE ε4, intracranial volume (ICV), and scanning site as nuisance variables.
evidence: The manuscript lists all predictors and covariates in SVC models.

claim: Non-parametric one-way ANOVA analyses were performed to test whether there was group differences across cognitive stages and across different pathology groups for each network.
source: To compare the brain metabolic and structural network scores between different cognitive stages and differenct pathology groups (Figure 1, step 3), we performed separate non-parametric one-way ANOVA analyses (5000 permutations, alpha = 0.05) to test whether there was group differences across cognitive stages and across different pathology groups for each network
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical method for group comparisons.

claim: Bonferroni-Holm correction was performed for the three pair's t-tests with adjusted alpha = 0.05.
source: We performed Bonferroni-Holm correction for the three pair's t-tests (adjusted alpha = 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript describes the multiple comparison correction method.

claim: Nuisance variables including age, gender, education years, APOE ε4, ICV, and scan site were regressed out from the network scores before non-parametric ANOVA.
source: The nuisance variables including age, gender, education years, APOE ε4, ICV, and scan site were regressed out from the network scores before non-parametric ANOVA.
evidence: The manuscript describes covariate adjustment for group comparisons.
